content: Fertility refers to the natural ability to conceive and give birth to offspring. The term fertility rate quantifies this by measuring the average number of children born per couple, individual, or population. It is distinct from fecundity, which describes the biological potential for reproduction, influenced by factors such as the production of gametes (eggs and sperm), successful fertilization, and the ability to carry a pregnancy to term. Historically, the term fertility was used primarily in reference to women, but as scientific understanding of reproduction has advanced, it is now applied to men as well, recognizing the critical role of male reproductive health. Infertility, on the other hand, is defined as a reduced or absent ability to conceive. Human fertility is influenced by a wide range of factors, including nutrition, sexual behavior, cultural norms, instinct, hormonal regulation, timing, economic conditions, lifestyle, and emotional well-being. Fertility in animals is similarly complex and often involves remarkable biological mechanisms. While it has traditionally been a reliable indicator of population growth, this is no longer the case in many parts of Asia. Factors such as selective abortion and gender imbalances have led to a decline in the ratio of women to men in certain populations. As a result, the traditional definition of fertility rate is no longer an accurate predictor of population growth in countries like China, India, and Myanmar. In humans, both men and women experience hormonal cycles that influence fertility. A woman’s menstrual cycle, which typically lasts about 28 days, determines when she is most likely to conceive. Men, on the other hand, do not have a fixed cycle but experience fluctuations in sperm quality, which researchers believe may be linked to internal hormonal rhythms. Age is another critical factor in fertility, particularly for women. Women are fertile for only about seven days during each menstrual cycle. Ovulation, the release of an egg from the ovary, occurs around the 14th day of the cycle, although the exact timing can vary. This is the most fertile period for women. If the egg is not fertilized by sperm, it will break down within 1–2 days and be reabsorbed by the body. However, sperm can survive in the female reproductive tract for up to five days. This means that conception is possible during a seven-day window: five days before ovulation and two days after. Female fertility peaks during the teenage years and begins to decline after the age of 30. For women attempting to conceive without the use of fertility treatments such as medications or in vitro fertilization (IVF), the likelihood of pregnancy decreases with age. At age 30, approximately 75% of women will conceive within one year, and 91% within four years. By age 35, these rates drop to 66% within one year and 84% within four years. At age 40, only 44% of women will conceive within one year, and 64% within four years. These statistics account for pregnancies that result in live births and reflect the increasing risk of miscarriage as women age. According to the March of Dimes, about 9% of recognized pregnancies in women aged 20–24 end in miscarriage. This risk rises to 20% for women aged 35–39 and exceeds 50% by age 42. The likelihood of birth defects, particularly those involving chromosomal abnormalities, also increases with maternal age. For example, the risk of having a baby with Down syndrome is approximately 1 in 1,250 at age 25, 1 in 1,000 at age 30, 1 in 400 at age 35, 1 in 100 at age 40, and 1 in 30 at age 45. Fertility treatments, including the use of fertility drugs and IVF, can improve the chances of conception at older ages. There have been documented cases of successful pregnancies in women as old as 67 with the help of fertility treatments. Medical professionals recommend that women over the age of 30 who have been unable to conceive after six months of trying should undergo fertility evaluation and testing.
